questions.prompt: In one sentence, what does a contract describe?
options: Who should do the work and when
What must become true, without assuming who makes it true
Which tool or model is required to do the work
How long the work should take
questions.explanation: A contract describes what must become true; it never assumes who executes it. That is what makes it executor-agnostic.

questions.prompt: This repository is a framework you install and run.
questions.explanation: It is documentation, not a framework. There is nothing to install — you read it, fork it, and drop its templates next to your own project.

questions.prompt: Why does writing work as an executor-agnostic contract help it survive changes in tooling?
options: Because contracts are written in a universal programming language
Because there is always someone doing the work, even as tools and models come and go
Because contracts are automatically translated between tools
Because the orchestrator rewrites contracts for each new tool
questions.explanation: Software outlives its tools. A contract independent of its executor survives every change of tooling, because there is always someone — or something — to execute it.

questions.prompt: Fork/join means the orchestrator splits work into parallel units that each commit or roll back, then recombines the committed results.
questions.explanation: Correct. The orchestrator forks work into parallel units of work; each commits or rolls back; the orchestrator joins the committed results.
